newsitem.title: USA: U.S. court ponders whether HIV is disability.
newsitem.headline: U.S. court ponders whether HIV is disability.

text.p: A federal appeals court heard arguments Friday on whether the Americans with Disabilities Act should apply to an estimated 650,000 people infected with the virus that causes AIDS, but who exhibit no symptoms.
The case stems from a Maine dentist's refusal to treat a woman infected with the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), but who was asymptomatic, in his Bangor office.

Dentist Randon Bragdon offered to treat the woman, Sydney Abbott, who needed a cavity filled and a cleaning, in a hospital setting even though he had no hospital affiliation at the time, court papers said.

Abbott then sued Bragdon, saying he had discriminated against her because of her HIV status, which a federal district judge found qualified under the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA). Bragdon then turned to the U.S. First Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston.
"This is a terribly difficult case," Circuit Judge Bruce Selya, one of the three members of the appeals court to hear the case, said from the bench.

"You have the interests and principles of great importance to the government, the people in this case ... and also you have to understand that people who practice the healing professions have certain protections as well," he said.

Samuel Bagenstos, a U.S. Justice Department attorney, argued in a brief on behalf of Abbott, "This case presents precisely the type of discrimination Congress had in mind when it passed the ADA. Randon Bragdon refused to provide Sydney Abbott with routine dental treatment in his office, and he did so solely because Abbott is HIV-positive."

The Centres for Disease Control, which estimates that up to 650,000 of the some 900,000 people infected with HIV are asymptomatic, has said, "The risk of transmission of HIV in a dental setting is so low as to be unquantifiable," according to court papers.
Abbott's lawyer David Webbert told the court: "The bottom line, your honour, is this is a question of science and all the scientific evidence is on our side."
Bragdon, in an interview after the hearing, said, "I'm not being forced to treat a patient. I'm being denied my ability to use my professional judgment."
